replacement: “Next we are lectured that our tribune is a tribune of true and sound ideas, and from this tribune of ‘sound ideas’ a solemn declaration is made that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is nothing but a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and if every child is to ask his father why he should love him, what will become of us? What will become of the foundations of society? What will become of the family? Parricide, it seems, is only a bogy for Moscow merchants’ wives. The most precious and most sacred guarantees for the destiny and future of Russian justice are laid before us in a twisted and frivolous form, all to reach a single aim—to justify something that cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the counsel for the defense. But mercy is all the criminal wants, and tomorrow we will see how crushed he is. And is the counsel for the defense not too modest in asking only that the prisoner be acquitted? Why not found a charity in honor of the parricide, to keep his exploit in memory for generations to come? Religion and the Gospel are corrected—all that is mysticism, we are told, and ours is the only true Christianity, the one that has been put to the test of reason and common sense. And so a false image of Christ is set up before us! ‘With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again,’ cried the counsel for the defense, and he instantly concludes that Christ teaches us to measure as it is measured to us—and this from the tribune of truth and sound sense! We look into the Gospel only on the eve of making speeches, to dazzle the audience with our acquaintance with a book that is, at any rate, a rather original composition, and may be useful for creating a certain effect—all to serve our purpose! But what Christ commands us is something very different. He bids us beware of doing this, because the wicked world does it. We ought to forgive and to turn the other cheek, and not to measure out to our persecutors what they measure out to us. This is what our God has taught us. He did not teach us that forbidding children to murder their fathers is a prejudice. And we will not, from the tribune of truth and good sense, correct the Gospel of our Lord, Whom the counsel for the defense condescends to call only ‘the crucified lover of humanity,’ in defiance of all orthodox Russia, which cries out to Him, ‘For You are our God!’”

At this the President broke in and reined in the over-eager speaker. He begged him not to exaggerate, not to go beyond the proper limits, and so on, the way presidents always do in such cases. The audience was uneasy too. The public was restless, and there were even shouts of indignation. Fetyukovitch did not so much as reply. He only stepped up to the tribune, laid his hand on his heart and, in an offended voice, spoke a few dignified words. Once more he touched lightly and ironically on “romancing” and “psychology,” and at a fitting moment he quoted, “Jupiter, you are angry, therefore you are wrong.” This drew a burst of approving laughter from the audience, since Ippolit Kirillovitch was nothing like Jupiter. Next, _à propos_ of the charge that he was teaching the young generation to murder their fathers, Fetyukovitch declared with great dignity that he would not even reply. As for the prosecutor’s accusation of unorthodox opinions, Fetyukovitch hinted that this was a personal insinuation. He had expected, he said, to be safe in this court from charges “damaging to my reputation as a citizen and a loyal subject.” At those words the President stopped him as well, and Fetyukovitch ended with a bow, to a murmur of approval through the courtroom. And Ippolit Kirillovitch was, in the view of our ladies, “crushed for good.”

“It would be shameful, disgraceful, not to acquit him!” cried the official. “Say he did murder him—there are fathers and fathers! Besides, he was in such a frenzy.... He may really have done nothing more than swing the pestle through the air and knock the old man down. But it was a pity they dragged the valet in. That was just an absurd theory! If I’d been in Fetyukovitch’s place, I would have said it straight out: ‘He murdered him, but he isn’t guilty, hang it all!’”

“Of course he didn’t tell you. It was that plan of escape. He had explained the main idea to me three days earlier, and we started quarreling over it at once, and we went on for three days. We quarreled because he said that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch were convicted, he would get him abroad together with that creature. I was furious at once. I can’t tell you why, I don’t know myself why.... Oh, of course I was furious about that creature, and that she should go abroad with Dmitri, too!” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly, her lips quivering with anger. “The moment Ivan Fyodorovitch saw I was furious about that woman, he decided I was jealous of Dmitri and still loved him. That is how our first quarrel started. I wouldn’t explain, and I couldn’t ask his forgiveness. I couldn’t bear that such a man could suspect me of still loving that ... when I had told him myself, long before, that I did not love Dmitri, that I loved no one but him! It was only my resentment of that creature that made me angry with him. Three days later, on the evening you came, he handed me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh, he saw his illness coming! He said the envelope held the details of the escape, and if he died or fell dangerously ill, I was to save Mitya, and only Mitya. Then he left me money, nearly ten thousand. Those are the banknotes the prosecutor mentioned in his speech, when he had heard from someone that Ivan had sent them to be changed. It struck me tremendously that Ivan Fyodorovitch had not given up on saving his brother, and that he trusted me with the plan of escape, even though he was still jealous of me and still sure I loved Mitya. Oh, that was a sacrifice! No, you can’t understand how great such self-sacrifice is, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence. But then it came to me that he would take it only as joy at the thought of Mitya being saved (and he certainly would have thought so!). The mere possibility of such an unjust thought in his head made me so angry that I lost my temper again. Instead of kissing his feet, I flew into a rage again! Oh, I am unhappy! It’s my character, my awful, unhappy character! Oh, you’ll see, I will end by driving him away, too, for another woman he can get on with better, as Dmitri did. But ... no, I couldn’t bear it, I would kill myself. And when you came in then, and I called out to you and told him to come back, the look of contempt and hatred he gave me enraged me so much that—do you remember?—I cried out to you that it was he, he alone, who had convinced me his brother Dmitri was a murderer! I said that spiteful thing on purpose, to hurt him again. He had never, never convinced me that his brother was a murderer. On the contrary, it was I who convinced him! Oh, my vile temper caused everything! I paved the way for that hideous scene at the trial. He wanted to prove to me that he was an honorable man, and that even if I loved his brother, he would not destroy him out of revenge or jealousy. So he came to the court ... I am the cause of it all, I alone am to blame!”

“It can be, and it ought to be!” Alyosha began forcefully, growing more animated. “He needs you very much just now. I wouldn’t have brought it up and upset you if it weren’t necessary. He is ill, he is beside himself, and he keeps asking for you. He doesn’t want you so that he can make peace with you. He only wants you to come and show yourself at his door. So much has happened to him since that day. He understands that he has wronged you beyond measure. He doesn’t ask your forgiveness—‘It’s impossible to forgive me,’ he says himself—he only asks that you appear in his doorway.”
“So you will come,” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I’ll go and tell him you’re coming right away.”
